Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Apply explicit corrections to the final stated intent. Preserve meaningful filler-like words and unfinished thoughts. Apply clearly spoken punctuation and list cues. Keep the supplied language.", "input": "On Tuesday morning, the records team began moving the shared project library from the old Northstar drive to the new Cedar workspace. The move covers current project folders, approved templates, meeting notes, and the reference archive used by the support and research groups. It does not include personal folders or the finance department’s restricted material. We are keeping the old drive available in read-only mode while people check the copied files, so nobody needs to change their bookmarks during the first week. The migration is being done in stages rather than as one overnight transfer because several teams have active work in the library, and the folder permissions need to be checked as carefully as the documents themselves.

The first stage covered the design and field research folders. Before copying, Nina compared the folder inventory with the spreadsheet that each group had updated on Friday. We found two folders with different names in the spreadsheet and on the drive, but their contents and owners matched, so Nina recorded the discrepancy in the migration log rather than creating duplicate folders. A handful of older meeting notes had no listed owner. Those stayed in the archive area, where the records team can review them without guessing who should have access. The copy preserved the original modified dates and file names. It also produced a report of shortcuts that pointed back to the old drive, which we will replace after each group confirms that its new folder opens correctly.

1. The team will use the migration log as the shared record of each batch. It includes the source path, destination path, copy time, number of files, permission check, and the name of the person who reviewed the result. The log is stored in the Cedar workspace, with edit access limited to the records team and view access for the project leads. If a reviewer finds a missing file or an unexpected access setting, they add a note to the relevant batch instead of making an unrecorded change. That gives us one place to see what has been checked and what still needs attention.

2. Project leads have three working days to review their folders. They should open a selection of documents, confirm that the files are current, and check that the people who need access can open them. A successful copy does not by itself confirm that the permissions are right. The design group, for example, has a mix of internal working files and material shared with two outside studios. Its lead is checking both kinds of access, and the outside studios should see only the folders that were shared with them before the move. If the Cedar workspace shows a person who should not have access, the lead should note the folder and contact records rather than changing the group settings independently.

3. The support team has a separate review because its reference archive contains older instructions that still appear in customer replies. Morgan is comparing the copied versions with the team’s current index and flagging pages that have been superseded. The old wording is not being deleted from the archive; it is being marked so that staff can distinguish an earlier instruction from the current one. Morgan said, “I found one answer that still points to the spring checklist, even though the fall checklist is the one we use now.” That page has been added to the review list. The team has not yet confirmed whether any other customer-facing links point to older material.

The second transfer batch is scheduled for Thursday afternoon and includes the communications and operations folders. Before it starts, the records team will check that the destination has enough space and that the scheduled copy job still uses the approved file filter. The filter excludes temporary cache files, but it includes spreadsheets, presentations, image files, and signed project documents. If the space check shows less than the planned reserve, the batch will be postponed and the project leads will be told before the scheduled start time. That condition matters because the team should not split a folder across two destinations just to keep the calendar date. At present, the workspace report shows enough available space, though the final check has not been run.

There are a few practical details for people working during the staged move. A document that is open during copying may appear in the report as skipped or changed after the copy begins. The records team will rerun those items after the owner closes the document, then add the new report to the batch log. Team members should keep editing active project material in its existing location until their lead confirms that the Cedar folder has passed review. The read-only period on the old drive is not starting for every group at once; each group will receive its own date after its review is complete. This avoids a situation where one group assumes a folder is ready because another group has already switched over.

The records team is also tracking a few questions that are not blockers for the current batches. One is whether the archive should keep both the original scanned forms and the searchable copies created last year. For now, both versions are included, and the archive index records which file is searchable. Another question concerns three project folders whose names include the same client abbreviation. Their leads have confirmed that the folders belong to separate projects, so they will keep their current names and remain under their respective project areas. We are not combining them or changing their ownership as part of this move. The team will note any further naming questions in the log and ask the relevant lead before altering a path.

At the end of each review window, the project lead will send the records team either a list of specific issues or a confirmation that the folder has been checked. That message is part of the review record, but it does not replace the file and permission checks recorded for the batch. When a group is ready to switch, the records team will update its shortcut, tell the group where the Cedar folder is, and keep the old location available in read-only mode according to the staged schedule. Until then, both locations have a defined role: the old drive remains the working location for groups still under review, while Cedar holds the copied material and the migration log.
